guides.title: Greenland / Kalaallit Nunaat — homelands, farms and colonial harbours
guides.description: From early Arctic camps to Inuit communities, Norse settlements and nineteenth-century connections.
guides.intro: Greenland has several intersecting human histories. Norse farms are one part of an Arctic landscape occupied by earlier peoples and by Inuit whose histories continue. Follow camps, fjords, exchange, changing settlement and colonial institutions without turning the island into a single European possession on every date.
guides.scope: Earliest supported regional evidence through 1900. Modern discovery, conservation and reference-map information retain their actual dates. This is selected evidence, not a complete census of every community or event.

map.scope: The whole regional area, with modern terrain and coastlines. Point dates refer to historical evidence; the relief does not reconstruct ancient ice, sea level or political control.

points.label: Norse Eastern Settlement, southwestern Greenland
points.date: Early eleventh-century context; short-lived archaeological samples at L'Anse aux Meadows broadly 990–1050, with cutting activity independently fixed to 1021
points.description: Norse seafarers connected Greenland's settlements with L'Anse aux Meadows on Newfoundland's northern peninsula. The line is a broad source-region connection. It does not date arrival to 1021, identify the crew as Leif's, or confirm a sequence of Labrador/Baffin landfalls. The 990–1050 window brackets context, not a sixty-year voyage.

points.label: Igaliku/Garðar, southern Greenland
points.date: Igaliku wood contexts: phase 1, 1100–1300 CE; phase 2, 1300–1400 CE
points.description: Small amounts of imported wood reached the bishop's farm at Igaliku alongside local wood and driftwood. A particular American forest, landing, ship, intermediary or annual shipment cannot be identified. The later phase contains potentially mixed deposits. No named transatlantic route is plotted from this point.

points.label: Western Greenland and eastern Canadian Arctic walrus-source region
points.date: Mid- and late-twelfth-century contexts, shown conservatively at century resolution
points.description: Walrus remains excavated in Kyiv connect its ivory supply with the western Arctic and Norse Greenland's trade network. The biological source is a wide region. Norse Greenland transit is an archaeological-historical inference; individual hunters, intermediaries, European ports and the complete route to Kyiv are not identified.

points.label: Qassiarsuk/Brattahlíð and the Eastern Settlement
points.date: Circa 985 to the mid-fifteenth century, regional Eastern Settlement chronology
points.description: Norse farming around Qassiarsuk belongs to the Eastern Settlement, whose regional occupation continued into the mid-fifteenth century. The 1450 marker is an inferred, approximate regional abandonment anchor. It is neither the proven date of the last departure nor a dated ending for each Qassiarsuk farm.

points.label: Jørgen Brønlund Fjord, Peary Land
points.date: circa 2400–1800 BCE; museum chronology for the principal Peary Land phase
points.description: Early communities camped around Jørgen Brønlund Fjord and hunted muskoxen, seals and birds. The dates describe a regional archaeological phase. Scattered later determinations do not justify continuous occupation of every camp. This does not identify Greenland's first individual landing.

points.label: Qeqertasussuk, southern Disko Bay
points.date: circa 2400–1400 BCE, the site-study chronology cited by the museum
points.description: Qeqertasussuk preserves tools, wood and animal remains from Saqqaq people living from the rich resources of Disko Bay. This broad site phase is not continuous residence by a single household, and the modern point is deliberately generalized.

points.label: Nipisat island, south of Sisimiut
points.description: Nipisat's hearths and animal remains record repeated seasonal visits by Saqqaq hunters over more than a millennium. The problematic 520 BCE determination is excluded. The encompassing interval is not year-round or uninterrupted residence.

points.label: Qilakitsoq, Uummannaq area
points.description: Two graves at Qilakitsoq preserve the clothing and personal histories of eight Inuit people. The approximate date concerns these burials; it does not date all houses at Qilakitsoq, identify the cause of death, or imply an end to Inuit life.

points.label: Historic harbour, Nuuk
points.date: 1728, construction date in the protected-building register
points.description: Hans Egede's house at Nuuk dates to 1728, marking a durable colonial mission establishment on this inhabited coast. The house's construction is not the beginning of Indigenous occupation. The 1721 mission is a different locality.

points.label: Igaliku, southern Greenland
points.description: Tuperna, Anders Olsen and their family established themselves at Igaliku in 1782 after farming at Upernaviarsuk. This is a dated family relocation and farming anchor; it does not imply direct continuity between the medieval Norse and eighteenth-century farms.

points.label: Historic harbour, Nuuk
points.date: 1850, construction date in the protected-building register
points.description: A provision store built at Nuuk in 1850 anchors the town's harbour-based supply and trade economy. The building date alone does not establish a specific cargo, overseas source port or trade volume.

points.label: Western Settlement, inner fjords of the present Nuuk region
points.date: Late tenth / early eleventh century to approximately the middle of the fourteenth century
points.description: The Western Settlement has both an approximate beginning and an approximate abandonment, around a century before the Eastern Settlement. The point represents a fjord region, not modern Nuuk town or a single excavated farm. No destination is inferred for departing residents.

points.label: Hvalsey church / Qaqortukulooq, Eastern Settlement
points.description: A precisely dated written event within a settlement whose final abandonment is less precisely known. No departure track or final population count is supplied. The exact date belongs to the wedding; it should not lend false day-level precision to settlement decline.

points.label: Disko Bay
points.date: About 600 BCE–200 CE in the Disko Bay middens
points.description: Dorset-associated tools and dwelling evidence record another chapter of life around Disko Bay.

points.label: Dove Bugt
points.date: About 200 BCE to the start of the Common Era
points.description: Dove Bugt preserves coastal finds related to the Independence II archaeological tradition.

points.label: Northwest Greenland / Thule region
points.description: The ancestors of present-day Greenlanders reached Greenland around 1200. Approximate museum chronology; no exact landing year or traced route is known.

points.label: Kangeq / Håbets Ø
points.description: Hans Egede’s party landed in Greenland on 3 July 1721. Approximate island anchor; the marker does not imply Danish control of the whole island.

points.label: Nipisat Sound near Kangeq
points.description: Egede recorded large groups traveling north in women’s boats in April 1722. A contemporary observation of people passing, not an annual population count or an exact boat track.

points.label: Ivittuut
points.description: Mining at Ivittuut connected Greenland to industrial demand for cryolite.

points.label: Peary Land and adjacent northern Greenland
points.description: Early Independence II dates occur in Peary Land and northeastern Greenland.

points.label: Northwestern Greenland, Nares Strait reference
points.description: Separate Late Dorset evidence occurs in northwestern Greenland in a later period than the Disko Bay horizon.

points.label: Kalaallit Nunaat / Greenland, island-wide reference
points.description: The ancestors of present-day Greenlandic Inuit communities reached Greenland around 1200, and Inuit communities continue beyond this timeline.

points.label: Tasiilaq / Ammassalik, east Greenland
points.description: A trade and mission station opened in 1894 in a region already inhabited by Tunumiit.

paragraphs.text: The early camp sites in this guide precede the Norse by millennia. Qeqertasussuk preserves unusually rich organic material, while Nipisat records repeated visits within a dated sequence. Such finds tell us about technologies and resource use without supplying a continuous population count.

Early Dorset and Independence II describe patterns in material evidence. The Disko Bay midden chronology covers approximately 600 BCE to 200 CE. Earlier Independence II evidence near 800–600 BCE belongs to northern contexts, while Dove Bugt has some younger dates. A later Dorset record in the High Arctic belongs to another period. Archaeological categories and dated finds do not give an annual population history.

The Greenland National Museum places the arrival of Thule ancestors around 1200. This was a broad Arctic movement associated with hunting, technology and travel. Inuit community life continued into the colonial period and beyond 1900. Regional histories include changes in where people lived and how they moved. This continuity is independent of the ending of Norse farming settlements in southwest Greenland.

sections.heading: Eastern and Western are names within southwest Greenland

paragraphs.text: Both Norse settlement districts lie in the southwest. The Western Settlement was in the Nuuk fjords; the Eastern Settlement lay farther south around present-day Kujataa. Their names do not describe settlements on the island’s opposite coasts.

Farming, herding, hunting and imported materials supported Norse households. Church sites and wealthy farms were connected to smaller holdings. Greenland’s museum presents these as communities with varied work, not simply as exploration bases.

sections.heading: What the retreat dates actually mean

paragraphs.text: Around 1350 and around 1450 are useful regional abandonment anchors for the Western and Eastern settlements. They are not known last-departure days. Hvalsey’s wedding in 1408 is a surviving written event; occupation evidence continued after that document. The movie retains the earlier places while identifying the loss of supported Norse occupation.

Changes in climate, relative sea level, grazing, maritime access and exchange are investigated with different evidence. They should not be compressed into one demonstrated cause of the settlements’ end. A regional decline also need not have happened identically at every farm.

The preserved people at Qilakitsoq make clothing and family histories unusually tangible. Their approximate fifteenth-century date belongs to Inuit history, not the chronology of Norse abandonment. The separate cold-preservation study examines what these remains can and cannot tell us.

sections.heading: A colony enters an inhabited landscape

paragraphs.text: The 1721 venture and the later Nuuk buildings mark new colonial institutions. Egede’s own account also witnessed substantial Indigenous movement near Kangeq. A colonial arrival therefore belongs beside an existing network of gathering places and travel.

The provision store at Nuuk, farming at Igaliku and cryolite at Ivittuut represent distinct economic histories. Tasiilaq’s 1894 trade and mission station altered conditions for existing Tunumiit communities in the east. These dates identify institutions or workplaces. The 1900 display ceiling does not describe the ending of the mine or any community.

guides.title: Iceland — settlement, assemblies and an enduring population
guides.description: Follow the settlement landscape, legal institutions, church, trade and nineteenth-century Reykjavík.
guides.intro: Iceland’s story continues after the end of Norse farming in Greenland. Archaeological settlement evidence, medieval texts and later administrative records let us follow different kinds of change while keeping the continuity of Iceland’s population in view.
guides.scope: Earliest supported regional evidence through 1900. Modern discovery, conservation and reference-map information retain their actual dates. This is selected evidence, not a complete census of every community or event.

map.scope: The whole regional area, with modern terrain and coastlines. Point dates refer to historical evidence; the relief does not reconstruct ancient ice, sea level or political control.

points.label: Hvammsfjörður region, western Iceland
points.date: circa 985 or 986 CE; historical tradition, not an exact sailing date
points.description: Households from Iceland established Norse farming settlements in southwestern Greenland around 985–986. No exact day, named embarkation beach or itinerary is known from this evidence. Both the Eastern and Western settlements were on Greenland's west side; this endpoint represents the Eastern Settlement.

points.label: Aðalstræti settlement site, Reykjavík
points.date: Wall predates the tephra dated about 871 ± 2 CE
points.description: An older wall beneath Reykjavík's later town preserves evidence from Iceland's settlement-period landscape.

points.label: Aðalstræti longhouse, Reykjavík
points.date: 930–1000 CE, museum chronology of the excavated hall
points.description: A turf-built longhouse at Aðalstræti records household life in tenth-century Reykjavík. The hall's archaeological dating does not identify its occupants by a saga name or date all nearby activity.

points.label: Þingvellir assembly site
points.description: Þingvellir hosted Iceland's assembly, bringing people together for law, disputes and political decisions. The interval does not mean uninterrupted independence or unchanged institutions. Visible ruins should not all be assigned to 930.

points.label: Skálholt, southern Iceland
points.description: Skálholt became an episcopal centre in 1056 and remained a major place of worship, learning and administration. The date applies to the institution and archaeological place, not to the present modern cathedral or uninterrupted operation of a particular school building.

points.label: Hafnarfjörður harbour
points.date: circa 1490–1602, German trading dominance before the Danish monopoly
points.description: Hafnarfjörður became an important harbour for German merchants trading with Icelanders. The period is approximate and does not date every merchant, building or voyage. No precise shipping track is inferred.

points.label: Aðalstræti 10, Reykjavík
points.description: Aðalstræti 10 was built for the Innréttingar enterprises in 1762, part of Reykjavík's growth as a place of manufacturing and work. This is a dated building within urban development, not the founding date of Reykjavík.

points.label: Iceland — island-wide population continuity
points.date: Settlement from around 870 CE; displayed through 1900
points.description: Iceland’s population continues while particular overseas Norse colonies end. The rounded point stands for the island, including its inhabited regions; it does not place an early farm in the interior. Continuity does not mean unchanged ancestry, institutions, religion or Viking-age culture.

points.label: Iceland — place described by Ari’s text, not an identified monastery
points.date: Íslendingabók composed circa 1122–1133; its papar story concerns an undated period before Norse settlement
points.description: A recorded tradition about possible Irish Christian predecessors, presented at the date of the text that attests it. The reference coordinate is only for Iceland as the subject of the narrative. It is not Ari’s writing desk, Papey monastery, a landing point, or a sailing destination. No precise arrival year or route is assigned.

points.label: Þingvellir
points.description: The adoption of Christianity is conventionally dated to around 1000. A historical convention sometimes given as 999/1000; conversion was a process.

points.label: Þingvellir
points.description: Agreements in 1262–1264 changed Iceland’s relationship to royal authority. The range covers acceptance of the agreement, not a single nationwide ceremony.

points.label: Þingvellir
points.description: The Jónsbók law code entered Iceland’s legal history in 1281. The assembly site is a reference for enactment, not the only place where the law was used.

points.label: Hólar
points.description: A press acquired around 1530 helped establish printing in Iceland. Approximate introduction date; it does not date every surviving edition.

points.label: Reykjavík regional reference
points.description: Royal restrictions governed Icelandic foreign trade from 1602 through 1787. Regional institutional anchor, not a single port’s complete shipping history.

points.label: Lakagígar
points.description: An eruption beginning in June 1783 continued into February 1784. Point marks the fissure region, not the footprint of lava, gases or famine.

points.label: Reykjavík, final meetings at Hólavallarskóli
points.description: Royal decree abolished the Alþingi in 1800.

points.label: Reykjavík
points.description: The restored assembly first met on 1 July 1845. 1843 authorized restoration; 1845 dates the first meeting.

points.label: Reykjavík
points.description: The 1874 constitution expanded Icelandic legislative responsibilities. The marker does not present 1874 as full independence.

points.label: Alþingishúsið, Reykjavík
points.description: Alþingi began meeting in its new stone building in 1881.

paragraphs.text: At Reykjavík the early wall fragment predates the tephra dated about 871 ± 2 CE. The ash constrains the age of evidence beneath it and the later longhouse has its own chronology. The settlement tradition and excavated remains have different dating evidence.

sections.heading: The papar: a tradition, not a traced voyage

paragraphs.text: Ari’s account describes Christian people said to have been present before the Norse. It was written centuries after the period it describes. We can map the production of the account and explain the claim; we cannot draw a documented Irish-monks itinerary from it.
Þingvellir provided a setting for an assembly from 930. Legal practice, meetings and the physical landscape changed over time. This was not a modern parliament with universal suffrage.

The adoption of Christianity and the creation of church institutions changed authority, education and material culture. Skálholt’s long history as a bishop’s seat is a separate sequence from any one conversion date.

The agreements of 1262–1264 brought Iceland under the Norwegian crown; Jónsbók followed in 1281. Local institutions continued under changed powers. A shared crown is a relationship between jurisdictions, not proof that their administration was identical.

Printing arrived around 1530. The museum’s account emphasizes religious publications and the use of Icelandic. Writing and printing expanded the ways texts circulated; they did not replace every oral or manuscript practice at once.

Hafnarfjörður’s German merchants belong to an earlier harbour history. The Danish monopoly from 1602 through 1787 was a later legal regime affecting foreign commerce. Neither interval establishes an exact ship route for every transaction.

sections.heading: A volcanic crisis with human witnesses

paragraphs.text: The Laki eruption of 1783–1784 is represented by its fissure-region anchor and by contemporary written accounts. Its consequences extended beyond the eruption site; a point is not an environmental impact boundary.

The final meeting at Þingvellir was in 1798. The assembly met in Reykjavík in 1799 and 1800 before it was abolished. A restored advisory parliament met in Reykjavík in 1845. Icelanders’ communities and daily activities continued across the changes in these institutions.

The 1874 constitution and the 1881 parliament building help place nineteenth-century political change in Reykjavík. Later home rule and sovereignty belong beyond this movie’s ceiling. The clock stops; the history does not.

guides.title: Faroe Islands — early livestock, ocean connections and local institutions
guides.description: A whole-archipelago study from pre-Norse evidence to the end of the trade monopoly and nineteenth-century change.
guides.intro: The Faroes sit within the sea routes connecting northern Britain, Norway, Iceland and Greenland. Their history includes early activity before the familiar Viking narrative, local assemblies and changing external crowns. Sea connections did not erase an island language or community.
guides.scope: Earliest supported regional evidence through 1900. Modern discovery, conservation and reference-map information retain their actual dates. This is selected evidence, not a complete census of every community or event.

map.scope: The whole regional area, with modern terrain and coastlines. Point dates refer to historical evidence; the relief does not reconstruct ancient ice, sea level or political control.

points.label: Eiðisvatn catchment, Eysturoy
points.description: Sheep DNA and fecal biomarkers indicate human introduction of livestock centuries before the familiar Norse settlement period.

points.label: Central Faroes / Streymoy
points.description: Norse settlement belongs to the ninth-century expansion across the North Atlantic.

points.label: Tinganes, Tórshavn
points.description: The conventional political chronology places the Faroes under the Norwegian crown in 1035. A retrospective constitutional anchor, not proof of uniform day-to-day control.

points.label: Tórshavn
points.description: The Faroes remained under the Danish crown when Norway passed into union with Sweden. Treaty relationship; not a claim that the islands had no local political life.

points.label: Tinganes, Tórshavn
points.description: Danish authorities abolished the Løgting in 1816. The map marks an institutional act, not the disappearance of Faroese identity.

points.label: Tórshavn regional reference
points.description: Hammersheimb developed an influential orthography for Faroese in 1846. City reference only; the marker is not the documented desk where the system was written.

points.label: Tórshavn
points.description: The Løgting was re-established with an advisory role in 1852. Institutional date; powers should be read in their nineteenth-century setting.

points.label: Tórshavn harbour
points.description: The end of the monopoly widened opportunities for Faroese commercial trade. The date is a legal change, not the beginning of all local exchange or a measured surge on every route.

points.label: Á Sondum, Sandoy
points.description: Two groups of peat ash and charred barley beneath later structures supply direct archaeological evidence of earlier Faroese activity.

sections.heading: Evidence before the Norse settlement period

paragraphs.text: Lake sediments at Eiðisvatn contain sheep DNA and fecal biomarkers that indicate livestock and human activity before ninth-century Norse settlement. The study dates the first signal to around 500 CE, within a range of 370–610 CE. Separately, charred barley from two peat ash layers at Á Sondum, on Sandoy, produced earlier and later calibrated ranges. Neither record identifies the communities responsible.

The published 95% interval is a dating result for the environmental signal. A broad bar on the timeline must not be read as continuous habitation throughout every year of that bar. The lake catchment is the evidence’s spatial setting, not a map of the entire early population.

sections.heading: Norse connections and an island society

paragraphs.text: Ninth-century settlement connected the archipelago with the wider Norse world. The local sequence should be kept distinct from later incorporation under a crown. Voyages, migration and political authority are separate layers.

The Faroes followed changing Norwegian and Danish crown relationships. The 1814 settlement retained them under Denmark while Norway entered its Swedish union. Their separate jurisdiction and cultural identity did not become an empty detail in that diplomatic change.

The assembly’s abolition in 1816 and restoration as an advisory body in 1852 mark institutional change. They do not imply equivalent political powers before and after, or a modern franchise in either period.

Hammersheimb’s orthography in 1846 belongs to a written-language history that drew on a continuing spoken language. The Tórshavn marker is a regional reference, not a claim that one building contains the whole story.

The royal monopoly ended in 1856. Fishing and export commerce expanded in the later nineteenth century, connecting changes in law with work at sea. This does not mean that exchange had been absent before the legal change.

Whole-island modern relief shows the physical setting of settlement and travel. Early evidence, institutional dates and harbour references have different precision. Blank years are gaps in this selected collection, not declarations that the islands were uninhabited.
